--- title: "Twenty Newsgroups" toc: true toc-depth: 4 toc-location: right sidebar: false --- ## About the Data This dataset contains approximately 20,000 Usenet discussion posts organized into 20 newsgroups covering topics such as computer hardware, science, sports, politics, religion, and vehicles. Originally collected by Ken Lang in 1995 for the Newsweeder system, the dataset provides a collection of real-world, user-generated text spanning a wide range of subjects, writing styles, and conversational patterns. Classifying text by topic is a common natural language processing (NLP) task that can help organize large collections of documents, categorize incoming messages, and make information easier to retrieve. However, text data often contains more than just the information relevant to the task. In addition to the main discussion, Usenet posts may contain structural metadata such as email headers, sender information, subject lines, quoted replies, and signatures. Although these elements may provide useful contextual information, they can also introduce noise or create misleading associations with the target category. As a result, a model may achieve high classification accuracy by recognizing metadata patterns rather than learning the actual subject matter of a discussion. This dataset provides an opportunity to investigate how text preprocessing influences model performance and the patterns learned from unstructured text. By comparing classification models trained and evaluated on raw and structurally cleaned posts, we can examine the extent to which metadata contributes to predictive performance and whether removing these shortcuts leads to more meaningful topic classification. We also explore whether unsupervised clustering can independently uncover meaningful topic groupings without access to the original category labels, and how these groupings compare with human-defined topics. ### Access the Data

### Variables ::: {.table-container} ::: {.styled-table} | Variable Name | Role | Type | Description | Missing Values | |-------------------|-----------|-------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------| | `doc_ID` | ID | Categorical | Unique document identifier (original Usenet file number) | No | | `category` | Target | Categorical | Original newsgroup category name (e.g., `alt.atheism`, `sci.space`) | No | | `text` | Feature | Text | Unmodified post text including routing headers, quotes, and body | No | ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ### Key Features of the Dataset Each record in this dataset corresponds to an individual Usenet discussion forum post and includes the following features and metadata: - **Identifier** (`doc_ID`) – ID number preserved from the original Usenet newsgroup archive within its category. - **Original Category** (`category`) – The specific Usenet newsgroup hierarchically labeled by netnews taxonomy (e.g., `alt.atheism`, `comp.graphics`, `rec.sport.hockey`, `sci.space`). - **Raw Text** (`text`) – Unmodified message content containing technical Usenet routing paths, sender email addresses, timestamps, quoted reply chains, and sign-offs. ### Purpose and Use Cases This dataset supports investigations into: - **Natural Language Processing & Text Classification:** Benchmarking classical and modern machine learning algorithms (Multinomial Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, Logistic Regression, neural networks) on high-dimensional sparse text data. - **Impact of Text Preprocessing Decisions:** Systematically evaluating how stripping structural artifacts (headers, quoted replies, signatures) affects model accuracy and lexical feature importance versus retaining raw metadata. - **Unsupervised Text Clustering:** Evaluating whether unsupervised clustering algorithms (such as K-Means, hierarchical clustering, and LDA topic modeling) naturally uncover the human-defined categories or organize documents according to writing style and shared conversational filler. ## Case Study ### Objective Text classification can help organize large volumes of unstructured information, but the quality and reliability of predictions depend heavily on how text is prepared. In this dataset, raw posts contain both topic-related discussions and structural elements such as email headers, sender affiliations, subject lines, and quoted replies. These elements may inadvertently reveal information about the original newsgroup category, allowing a model to achieve high classification accuracy by exploiting metadata rather than learning meaningful topical patterns from the discussion itself. In this case study, we will focus on several key questions: - How accurately can a Multinomial Naive Bayes model classify discussion posts into their original newsgroup categories using TF-IDF features? - To what extent does the removal of headers, quoted replies, and other structural artifacts affect classification performance, and does the raw text contain potential sources of data leakage that inflate model performance? - Can K-Means clustering identify meaningful topic groupings without access to the original category labels, and how do these groupings compare with the predefined categories? By comparing classification performance on raw and cleaned text, we can investigate how preprocessing affects model performance and identify potential data leakage arising from structural metadata. A model that performs well on raw text may not necessarily have learned the underlying topics. Instead, it may rely on superficial cues that happen to correlate with the target labels. We will also examine the patterns and limitations of unsupervised clustering to understand when automatically discovered groups align with human-defined topics and when they reflect shared vocabulary or writing styles instead. --- ### Analysis **Loading Libraries** ::: {.panel-tabset} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(knitr) library(stringr) library(purrr) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import tarfile from pathlib import Path import pandas as pd import numpy as np import re from IPython.display import Markdown # Visualizations import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns # NLP import nltk from nltk.corpus import stopwords from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer from nltk.tokenize import RegexpTokenizer for resource in ['corpora/wordnet', 'corpora/omw-1.4', 'corpora/stopwords']: try: nltk.data.find(resource) except LookupError: nltk.download(resource.split('/')[1], quiet=True) ``` ```{.python .cell-code} # Modeling from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report, ConfusionMatrixDisplay from sklearn.cluster import KMeans ``` ::: ::: #### 1. Let's map the 20 newsgroups into seven broader categories and assign human-readable names to each of the 20 original topics. This makes it easier to explore the dataset at both a broad thematic level and a more specific topic level. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} macro_mapping <- c( "alt" = "Religion & Beliefs", "comp" = "Computers & Tech", "misc" = "Miscellaneous", "rec.autos" = "Vehicles", "rec.motorcycles" = "Vehicles", "rec.sport" = "Sports", "sci" = "Science", "soc" = "Religion & Beliefs", "talk.politics" = "Politics", "talk.religion" = "Religion & Beliefs" ) topic_mapping <- c( "alt.atheism" = "Atheism", "comp.graphics" = "Graphics", "comp.os.ms-windows.misc" = "MS Windows", "comp.sys.ibm.pc.hardware" = "IBM PC Hardware", "comp.sys.mac.hardware" = "Mac Hardware", "comp.windows.x" = "X Windows", "misc.forsale" = "For Sale / Classifieds", "rec.autos" = "Automobiles", "rec.motorcycles" = "Motorcycles", "rec.sport.baseball" = "Baseball", "rec.sport.hockey" = "Hockey", "sci.crypt" = "Cryptography", "sci.electronics" = "Electronics", "sci.med" = "Medicine", "sci.space" = "Space", "soc.religion.christian" = "Christianity", "talk.politics.guns" = "Gun Politics", "talk.politics.mideast" = "Middle East Politics", "talk.politics.misc" = "General Politics", "talk.religion.misc" = "General Religion" ) get_macro <- function(cat) { if (str_starts(cat, "rec.autos")) return("Vehicles") if (str_starts(cat, "rec.motorcycles")) return("Vehicles") if (str_starts(cat, "rec.sport")) return("Sports") if (str_starts(cat, "talk.politics")) return("Politics") if (str_starts(cat, "talk.religion")) return("Religion & Beliefs") prefix <- str_split(cat, "\\.")[[1]][1] macro_mapping[[prefix]] } ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} macro_mapping = { 'alt': 'Religion & Beliefs', 'comp': 'Computers & Tech', 'misc': 'Miscellaneous', 'rec.autos': 'Vehicles', 'rec.motorcycles': 'Vehicles', 'rec.sport': 'Sports', 'sci': 'Science', 'soc': 'Religion & Beliefs', 'talk.politics': 'Politics', 'talk.religion': 'Religion & Beliefs' } topic_mapping = { 'alt.atheism': 'Atheism', 'comp.graphics': 'Graphics', 'comp.os.ms-windows.misc': 'MS Windows', 'comp.sys.ibm.pc.hardware': 'IBM PC Hardware', 'comp.sys.mac.hardware': 'Mac Hardware', 'comp.windows.x': 'X Windows', 'misc.forsale': 'For Sale / Classifieds', 'rec.autos': 'Automobiles', 'rec.motorcycles': 'Motorcycles', 'rec.sport.baseball': 'Baseball', 'rec.sport.hockey': 'Hockey', 'sci.crypt': 'Cryptography', 'sci.electronics': 'Electronics', 'sci.med': 'Medicine', 'sci.space': 'Space', 'soc.religion.christian': 'Christianity', 'talk.politics.guns': 'Gun Politics', 'talk.politics.mideast': 'Middle East Politics', 'talk.politics.misc': 'General Politics', 'talk.religion.misc': 'General Religion' } def get_macro_category(raw_cat): if raw_cat.startswith('rec.autos'): return macro_mapping['rec.autos'] elif raw_cat.startswith('rec.motorcycles'): return macro_mapping['rec.motorcycles'] elif raw_cat.startswith('rec.sport'): return macro_mapping['rec.sport'] elif raw_cat.startswith('talk.politics'): return macro_mapping['talk.politics'] elif raw_cat.startswith('talk.religion'): return macro_mapping['talk.religion'] else: prefix = raw_cat.split('.')[0] return macro_mapping.get(prefix, 'Other') ``` ::: ::: Before training our models, we also implement specialized text-cleaning functions to remove common sources of noise in Usenet posts. Unlike general text preprocessing, which often focuses on lowercasing words or removing punctuation, these functions target the structure of discussion posts: - **Remove headers:** Extracts the message body by removing the header section, which may contain information such as the sender, subject, and newsgroup. Although some header information may help identify a post's topic, relying on it could allow a model to learn from metadata rather than the content of the message. - **Remove quoted lines:** Removes lines that begin with common quotation markers, such as `>` or `|>`. Quoted text often repeats content from earlier messages, which may introduce irrelevant information or cause the same text to appear across multiple posts. - **Remove reply introductions:** Removes phrases such as “In article ... writes:” that introduce quoted replies. These lines describe the structure of a conversation rather than the topic being discussed. - **Combine the cleaning steps:** Applies the functions in sequence and trims leading and trailing whitespace to produce a cleaned version of each post. We preserve the original text so that we can compare model performance on raw and cleaned posts. We also record the character count before and after cleaning and calculate the percentage of text removed. Token-Level NLP Preprocessing To normalize the vocabulary for machine learning, we apply token-level preprocessing. In this case study, we will be applying the following: - **Case Normalization:** Lowercasing all characters. - **Tokenization & Punctuation Filtering:** Extracting alphabetic tokens of three or more characters (`\b[a-zA-Z]{3,}\b`), filtering out punctuation and single-letter abbreviations. - **Stopword Removal:** Eliminating ubiquitous English grammatical words (*the, is, at, which*). - **Lemmatization**: Converting words to their morphological base form (e.g., cities $\rightarrow$ city, cars $\rightarrow$ car). ::: {.panel-tabset} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nltk_tokenize <- import("nltk.tokenize") nltk_stem <- import("nltk.stem") nltk_corpus <- import("nltk.corpus") tokenizer_r <- nltk_tokenize$RegexpTokenizer("\\b[a-zA-Z]{3,}\\b") lemmatizer_r <- nltk_stem$WordNetLemmatizer() stop_words_r <- nltk_corpus$stopwords$words("english") preprocess_text_r <- function(text) { text <- as.character(text) text_lower <- str_to_lower(text) tokens <- tokenizer_r$tokenize(text_lower) filtered_tokens <- tokens[!tokens %in% stop_words_r] lemmatized_tokens <- vapply(filtered_tokens, lemmatizer_r$lemmatize, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE) str_c(lemmatized_tokens, collapse = " ") } df <- df |> mutate(nlp_clean_text = map_chr(clean_text, preprocess_text_r)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} tokenizer = RegexpTokenizer(r'\b[a-zA-Z]{3,}\b') lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer() stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english')) def preprocess_text(text): text = str(text).lower() tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text) cleaned_tokens = [ lemmatizer.lemmatize(word) for word in tokens if word not in stop_words ] return " ".join(cleaned_tokens) df["nlp_clean_text"] = df["clean_text"].apply(preprocess_text) ``` ::: ::: #### 5. Modelling - Can We Predict Discussion Topics from Text? We begin with supervised learning to investigate whether a discussion post's topic can be predicted from its text. As a starting point, we use Multinomial Naive Bayes, a simple and computationally efficient baseline model that works well with text data. Although Naive Bayes provides a useful starting point, it makes simplifying assumptions about how words contribute to a document's topic. More advanced approaches, such as logistic regression, support vector machines (SVMs), and ensemble methods, could be explored to improve classification performance. Neural networks and transformer-based models offer another direction for capturing more complex relationships and contextual information in text. Before training the model, let's first look at how Naive Bayes works and why it is commonly used for text classification. ##### 5.1 How Naive Bayes Works **The Learning Phase** When we call `fit()`, the model learns statistical patterns from the training documents rather than building complex rules for individual posts. It estimates two key components: Prior Probability: The probability of each category before considering the document's contents. For example, if 5% of the training documents belong to the Space category, the model estimates a prior probability of 5% for that category. Feature Likelihoods: The model estimates how strongly each word is associated with each category. For example, words such as "orbit" and "moon" are likely to have higher estimated likelihoods under the Space category than under the Hockey category. **The Prediction Phase** When we provide a new, unseen document, the model uses Bayes' Theorem to estimate how likely each category is given the document's features. The underlying idea can be expressed as: $$ P(\text{Category} \mid \text{Document}) \propto P(\text{Category}) \times P(\text{Document} \mid \text{Category}) $$ For a bag-of-words representation, the document likelihood is approximated using the individual word likelihoods: $$ P(\text{Document} \mid \text{Category}) \approx \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(\text{Word}_i \mid \text{Category}) $$ In other words, the model: - Starts with the prior probability of a category. - Considers the contribution of each word feature based on the patterns learned from documents in that category. - Combines these contributions to calculate a score for each category. - Repeats this process across all 20 categories and predicts the category with the highest resulting score. For example, if a post contains words such as "ice", "puck", and "goal", these features may collectively produce a higher score for the Hockey category than for the Space category. In this case study, documents are represented using TF-IDF rather than raw word counts. Each term is assigned a non-negative weight based on its frequency within a document and how informative it is across the corpus. These weights are used as input features by the Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier to estimate the likelihood of each topic. The probability equation above provides a simplified illustration of how the model combines evidence from individual terms. Since TF-IDF values are weighted features rather than literal word counts, the equation is intended to explain the underlying classification principle rather than represent every calculation performed by the implementation. **Why is it called "Naive"?** The model is considered "naive" because it makes a simplifying assumption: given a category, each word is treated as conditionally independent of the other words in the document. For example, if the model encounters the word "San", it does not account for the possibility that the next word might be "Francisco". It ignores word order, grammar, and relationships between words, treating each document as a collection of independent features (often described as a bag of words). Despite this simplifying assumption, Naive Bayes is computationally efficient and can perform surprisingly well on text classification tasks. ##### 5.2 Train-Test Split We perform an 80/20 train-test split, stratified by the original topic label (`stratify=y`). Stratification preserves the approximate distribution of all 20 categories in both sets, ensuring that the models are evaluated on a representative sample. We also use the same split for both raw and cleaned text. This ensures that the two pipelines are trained and evaluated using the same underlying posts, allowing us to make a more direct comparison of their performance. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sk_split <- import("sklearn.model_selection") sk_pipe <- import("sklearn.pipeline") sk_feature <- import("sklearn.feature_extraction.text") sk_nb <- import("sklearn.naive_bayes") sk_metrics <- import("sklearn.metrics") X_raw_r <- df$text X_clean_r <- df$clean_text y_r <- df$topic split_res <- sk_split$train_test_split( X_raw_r, X_clean_r, y_r, test_size = 0.2, random_state = 42L, stratify = y_r ) X_raw_train_r <- split_res[[1]] X_raw_test_r <- split_res[[2]] X_clean_train_r <- split_res[[3]] X_clean_test_r <- split_res[[4]] y_train_r <- split_res[[5]] y_test_r <- split_res[[6]] ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} X_raw = df["text"] X_clean = df["clean_text"] y = df["topic"] X_raw_train, X_raw_test, X_clean_train, X_clean_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X_raw, X_clean, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y ) ``` ::: ::: ##### 5.3 Building the Pipelines **Feature Extraction (TF-IDF Representation)** Before training the classifier, we need to convert the text into numerical features that a machine learning model can process. We use `TfidfVectorizer` from `scikit-learn` to build a vocabulary and calculate Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) scores. **TF-IDF** is a statistical method that estimates how important a word is to an individual document relative to the entire collection of documents (the corpus). It combines two components: **Term Frequency (TF)**: Measures how frequently a word appears in a particular document. A word that appears frequently in a post receives a higher term frequency score. **Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)**: Measures how common or rare a word is across the entire corpus. Words that appear in many documents receive lower weights, while words that appear in fewer documents receive higher weights. Combining these two components gives greater weight to words that are relatively frequent within a particular post but less common across the dataset. This helps distinguish documents based on their more informative terms. **Parameters** We use document frequency thresholds (`min_df` and `max_df`) to filter out extremely rare and overly common terms. We also limit the vocabulary size to keep the feature space manageable. - `max_features=5000`: Limits the vocabulary to the 5,000 terms with the highest overall term frequency, helping reduce memory usage and computational complexity. - `min_df=5` (Minimum Document Frequency): Excludes terms that appear in fewer than five documents. This helps filter out typos, unique usernames, and other terms that may not generalize well. - `max_df=0.7`(Maximum Document Frequency): Excludes terms that appear in more than 70% of the documents. These terms are generally too common to be useful for distinguishing between topics. **Training Two Parallel Pipelines** We train two independent pipelines to investigate how structural text cleaning affects classification: 1. **Raw Pipeline:** Trained on the original posts, including Usenet headers, subject lines, sender information, and other structural metadata. 2. **Clean Pipeline:** Trained on structurally cleaned posts, with headers, quoted lines, and reply introductions removed. Each pipeline learns its own TF-IDF vocabulary and feature weights from its respective training data. This allows us to examine how removing structural information changes the features available to the classifier and its ability to predict discussion topics. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_pipe_r <- sk_pipe$Pipeline(list( tuple("tfidf", sk_feature$TfidfVectorizer(max_features = 5000L, min_df = 5L, max_df = 0.7)), tuple("clf", sk_nb$MultinomialNB()) )) clean_pipe_r <- sk_pipe$Pipeline(list( tuple("tfidf", sk_feature$TfidfVectorizer(max_features = 5000L, min_df = 5L, max_df = 0.7)), tuple("clf", sk_nb$MultinomialNB()) )) raw_pipe_r$fit(X_raw_train_r, y_train_r) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pipeline(steps=[('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(max_df=0.7, max_features=5000, min_df=5)), ('clf', MultinomialNB())]) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} clean_pipe_r$fit(X_clean_train_r, y_train_r) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pipeline(steps=[('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(max_df=0.7, max_features=5000, min_df=5)), ('clf', MultinomialNB())]) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Predictions across evaluation scenarios y_pred_raw_on_raw_r <- raw_pipe_r$predict(X_raw_test_r) y_pred_raw_on_clean_r <- raw_pipe_r$predict(X_clean_test_r) y_pred_clean_on_clean_r <- clean_pipe_r$predict(X_clean_test_r) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} raw_pipeline = Pipeline([ ('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(max_features=5000, min_df=5, max_df=0.7)), ('clf', MultinomialNB()) ]) clean_pipeline = Pipeline([ ('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(max_features=5000, min_df=5, max_df=0.7)), ('clf', MultinomialNB()) ]) raw_pipeline.fit(X_raw_train, y_train) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

However, this high accuracy may be partly explained by metadata shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of the discussion topics. For example, the raw posts contain several features that can reveal the target category: - **Newsgroups headers:** These may explicitly contain the category label (e.g., `rec.sport.hockey`). - **Subject lines:** These frequently contain keywords that directly indicate the discussion topic. - **Sender and organization information:** Email domains and affiliations (e.g., `cmu.edu`, `nasa.gov`, `mit.edu`) may be associated with particular topics. When we evaluate the raw model on cleaned test posts, accuracy drops from 88% to 73%. This suggests that the raw model relied, at least in part, on structural information that was removed during preprocessing, and that its performance is sensitive to changes in the text representation. Through supervised classification, we found that retaining raw Usenet text can produce deceptively high accuracy, partly because structural metadata provides shortcuts that reveal information about the original categories. After removing headers, quoted replies, and other structural artifacts, the Multinomial Naive Bayes model achieved approximately 73% accuracy across the twenty specific topics. However, accuracy increased to approximately 86% when predictions were evaluated across the seven broader categories. This suggests that even when the model struggles to distinguish between closely related topics, it can still recognize their broader thematic domains. The unsupervised clustering analysis provided a complementary perspective. Without access to the original category labels, K-Means identified several recognizable topical groupings, including sports, computer hardware, automobiles, cryptography, and political discussions. However, the discovered clusters did not consistently align with the predefined categories. Some combined related discussions, while others captured general conversational language or communication patterns rather than specific subjects. Both the R and Python workflows revealed similar broad patterns, although their exact cluster compositions should be interpreted in the context of their underlying preprocessing and implementation. Together, these findings highlight the importance of thoughtful text preprocessing and careful model evaluation. High classification accuracy does not necessarily indicate that a model has learned meaningful relationships, particularly when structural features can act as shortcuts. Similarly, unsupervised clustering can reveal useful patterns in unstructured text, but the resulting groupings depend on how documents are represented and do not necessarily reflect human-defined topics.
